oil.summary: Crude is under heavy pressure across the complex, with Brent off 2.23% today to $89.90/bbl and WTI slipping to $82.86 — both down sharply on the month (Brent -17%, WTI -15%). The divergence between active geopolitical risk and falling prices reflects a supply-side offset: the US temporarily eased Russia sanctions and struck a reported $7bn Russian diesel deal, adding barrels to the market. Brazilian offshore production is booming, adding more supply than any other country this year. Meanwhile, Iran mounted roughly 14 Hormuz attacks in November, striking at least one tanker twice, yet market reaction has been muted. CME options now price a 77% chance of an OPEC cut at the May 2026 meeting, underscoring weak demand sentiment. Trump's pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries adds further political complexity as Ukrainian attacks are reported to have nearly halved Russian refining capacity this month.
drivers: US temporary easing of Russia oil sanctions floods additional supply into the market, capping geopolitical risk premiums despite Hormuz tanker strikes
Brazil's offshore production boom accelerating global supply growth, adding downward price pressure on a one-month basis (-15% WTI, -17% Brent)
CME options pricing 77% probability of OPEC production cut at May 2026 meeting, signalling persistent demand-side weakness

gas.summary: Henry Hub retreated sharply, falling 4.00% on the day to $3.237/MMBtu, though it remains 16% higher on the month — a reminder of the significant run-up in recent weeks now partially unwinding. TTF moved in the opposite direction, surging 4.46% to €84.45/MWh, though it is still down 8.46% on the week. The TTF bounce likely reflects lingering Middle East supply anxiety, with headlines flagging that the Iran conflict caused the largest oil and gas disruption on record and a drone incident at an Iraqi gas field adding to jitters. A notable structural story: Canada is actively building LNG export infrastructure to diversify away from US customers following tariff friction, a shift that could redraw North American gas trade flows. News flow for this sector is relatively thin today beyond these themes.
drivers: Henry Hub selling off 4% intraday as the month-long rally cools, while TTF gains 4.46% on residual Middle East supply disruption fears
Iran conflict described as causing the largest oil and gas disruption on record, with an Iraqi gas field drone incident adding regional risk
Canada accelerating LNG export infrastructure buildout to reduce dependence on US market, a potential long-term structural shift in North American gas flows

power.summary: EU Carbon EUAs suffered a sharp 8.28% single-day drop to $76.25/EUA, extending a painful week (-10.74%) and month (-6.41%). The move is notable in magnitude; no specific headline directly explains today's sell-off, suggesting macro risk-off and the broader energy complex decline may be dragging carbon lower. TTF's 4.46% daily gain creates a cross-current: higher gas prices typically support carbon by incentivising fuel-switching to coal, but the month-long TTF softness may already be weighing on longer-dated carbon sentiment. On the demand side, new data quantifying US data-centre power consumption is described as 'staggering,' reinforcing the structural AI-driven power demand thesis. Egypt's plan to bring 7,000 factories onto solar power as part of a 42%-renewables-by-2030 target adds a supply-side decarbonisation datapoint. Headlines for the power and carbon sector are otherwise limited today.
drivers: EU Carbon EUAs down 8.28% on the day and nearly 11% on the week — the sharpest move across all monitored sectors — with no single headline catalyst identified
AI-driven US data-centre power demand described as 'staggering' in new quantitative data, reinforcing the structural bull case for power consumption growth
Egypt targets 42% renewable electricity by 2030, with 7,000 factories moving to solar, illustrating accelerating non-EU clean energy buildout
